topics.name: Answering Comprehension Questions
topics.description: How to read a passage for answers: find the topic sentence, tap the evidence, then choose. Covers inference, mood, attitude, figures of speech and idiom in context.

topics.name: Summary Writing
topics.description: One passage, five questions, one summary. How to compress without losing the point, and how JAMB marks a summary.

topics.name: Description Passages
topics.description: Description gives a detailed picture of a person, place or thing. Recognising it tells you where to look for the topic sentence and the details.

topics.name: Narration Passages
topics.description: Narration tells a sequence of events. Plot, turning point and the narrator’s attitude carry most of the answers.

topics.name: Exposition Passages
topics.description: Exposition explains a process, a cause or a comparison. Signposting words carry the logic, and the answers hide inside them.

topics.name: Argumentation and Persuasion
topics.description: Argumentation defends a position. Learn to spot the claim, the concession and the rhetorical question, and to read the writer’s opinion rather than your own.

topics.name: The Cloze Test
topics.description: Ten questions from one gapped passage. The gaps are grammar questions wearing a passage costume — learn to read the gap, not the story.

topics.name: Synonyms
topics.description: Words with the same or nearly the same meaning. Also covers the trap: near-synonyms are not interchangeable in every context.

topics.name: Antonyms
topics.description: Opposites — and the harder grade question: which word is the opposite in this context, not in general.

topics.name: Clause and Sentence Patterns

topics.name: Word Classes and Their Functions
topics.description: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs and the rest — what each does in a sentence, and how function beats form when they disagree.

topics.name: Mood, Tense and Aspect
topics.description: Four tenses but three times: past, present, future — and the aspect that says whether the action is finished or ongoing.

topics.name: Number, Agreement and Concord

topics.name: Degrees of Comparison
topics.description: Positive, comparative and superlative — including the irregular forms and the one-word rule that catches most candidates.

topics.name: Question Tags
topics.description: The tag that closes a statement. Same tense, opposite polarity, and the fixed expressions that never change.

topics.name: Mechanics: Spelling and Punctuation
topics.description: Correct spelling and the punctuation marks JAMB tests — the apostrophe, the comma, the full stop, the colon.

topics.name: Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage
topics.description: The same word can be literal or figurative. Idioms tested are formal ones in Standard British English.

topics.name: Vowels: Monothongs, Diphthongs and Triphthongs
topics.description: One glide or two or three in a single vowel sound, and what changes when you add a suffix.

topics.name: Consonants and Consonant Clusters
topics.description: Place and manner of articulation, and the clusters that English stacks together without a vowel between them.

topics.name: Rhymes and Homophones

topics.name: Word Stress
topics.description: Which syllable carries the stress in a one-syllable or many-syllable word, and how suffixes move it.

lessons.title: Comprehension Tips
lessons.objective: A read-and-answer playbook: predict, underline, decide and eliminate to protect marks.

content.heading: Comprehension Tips
paragraphs: A read-and-answer playbook: predict, underline, decide and eliminate to protect marks.

bullets: Scan the questions in one sweep — they tell you what to look for.
Notice the question verbs: what (fact), why (reason), whom (person), how (manner).
Never guess an answer without checking the passage; every answer must be supported by the text.
content.heading: Before you read the passage
paragraphs: Do not read the passage first. Read the questions first so you know what to look for, then read the passage with those questions already in your mind. Every answer must come from the text, not from real-world knowledge.

bullets: Note the topic sentence of each paragraph — usually the first sentence.
Circle proper nouns, dates and figures; questions love to reuse them.
Slow down at signal words: however, but, therefore, because, in addition, for example.
If a word is unfamiliar, keep going — the surrounding words usually hint at its meaning.
content.heading: While you read
paragraphs: Read actively: underline the main idea of each paragraph and tick anything the questions asked about. Understanding where each idea sits makes finding answers fast.

bullets: Main idea: the option that covers the whole passage, not a single detail.
Tone/mood: match the emotional language of the passage (happy, critical, sarcastic, persuasive).
Vocabulary in context: replace the word with each option and see which fits the two lines around it.
Inference: the correct answer follows logically from the text; distractor options feel plausible but are not implied.
Reference ("it", "they"): look at the nearest earlier noun that fits grammatically.
Budget two minutes per question; leave hard ones and return to them.
content.heading: Question types and tactics
paragraphs: The most common question types follow the same logic every year. Match each question to its tactic:

bullets: Reject options with extreme words (always, never, everyone) — passages rarely support them.
Reject options that are true in real life but absent from the passage.
If two options look alike, re-read the supporting sentence; the correct one is usually the more specific.
content.heading: How to eliminate options
paragraphs: When you are stuck, eliminate rather than guess blindly. Wrong comprehension options usually leave a tell: an extreme word, real-world truth not in the passage, or vagueness.

content.body: Never leave a comprehension question blank. If stuck, pick the option with the strongest textual support — examiners reward exactness, not imagination.
content.title: Exam tip
Kolo Creek
content.purpose: what changed the village — and what the chairman really means

questions.question: In paragraph 1, “there was no money for a borehole” shows that the council’s failure was mainly one of
questions.explanation: The council met “several times to discuss the problem” — they knew about it. What stopped them was money, not ignorance or indifference.

questions.question: The word “fate” as used by the chairman in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: He contrasts “fate” with “a problem waiting for a plan” — the village had treated the shortage as something that could not be changed, when it could.

paragraphs: For many years, the residents of Kolo Creek depended entirely on a single hand-dug well. When the well ran dry each March, women and children walked over four kilometres to the next village to fetch water. The village council met several times to discuss the problem, but every meeting ended the same way: there was no money for a borehole.

Everything changed when a team of engineers visited the community as part of a rural water scheme. They tested the soil, sank a borehole near the primary school, and trained three young people to maintain the pump. Within a year, cases of water-borne illness reported at the health centre fell by more than half, and school attendance rose because children no longer spent their mornings fetching water.

The chairman of the council later admitted that the community had grown used to managing scarcity instead of solving it. “We treated the shortage as fate,” he said, “when it was only a problem waiting for a plan.” The borehole did not just bring water; it changed what the village believed was possible.

content.title: Rain at the Bus Park
content.purpose: the mood of the waiting passengers — and what the writer admires

questions.question: The writer’s attitude towards the stranded passengers is best described as
questions.explanation: Clues: “no grumbling”, “good humour”, “as though the delay had been a small festival”, and the closing praise of “a patience … no timetable can teach”.

paragraphs: The rain had been falling since dawn, drumming steadily on the zinc roof of the bus park. Passengers huddled under the narrow shed, watching the road turn slowly into a brown river. A hawker moved among them, balancing her tray with practised ease, calling out prices that nobody answered. Yet there was no grumbling; strangers shared umbrellas, and a boy laughed as his paper boat spun away down the gutter.

When the downpour finally eased, the driver clapped his hands and shouted that the journey would continue. People climbed aboard with damp clothes and good humour, as though the delay had been a small festival rather than an inconvenience. There is a patience in such moments that no timetable can teach.

content.prompt: You just answered with evidence tapped first. On Saturday, will you read the passage first or the questions first — and which sentence from Kolo Creek would you point to as proof your method works?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names one method (“questions first, so I know what to hunt for”), one reason tied to evidence (“because my taps on the council sentences decided Q1 before I read the options”), and one fallback (“if the passage is narrative like the bus park, I read for mood first”). If your answer has all three, your method is exam-ready; if not, borrow the missing piece.

content.title: The Blackout Proposal
content.purpose: whether the writer supports the shutdown — and where he places the blame

options.text: a punishment of the innocent that misses the cause
the only way to stop cheating centres
unfair only to traders and patients

questions.question: The writer’s position on the social media shutdown is that it is
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls it punishing “millions of innocent users” while syndicates “switch to offline methods”; paragraph 3 demands securing presses instead. The writer opposes it because it misses the cause.

options.text: unable to control the officials within their own system

questions.question: “It cannot police its own gates” (paragraph 3) implies that the authorities are
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the call to “prosecute the officials who sell” papers and closes with “the gatekeepers did” break the exam — the failure is internal, not technical.

paragraphs: Every examination season brings the same proposal: shut down social media until the last paper is written. Its supporters argue that leaked questions and coordinated cheating spread through phones faster than any invigilator can respond. They point to cancelled results and withheld scripts as proof that the examination system is bleeding, and they insist that a temporary blackout is a small price for credibility.

The proposal sounds decisive, but it mistakes the channel for the cause. Questions leak because printing and distribution chains are compromised long before candidates open an app; cheating centres operate with or without a network signal. A shutdown would punish millions of innocent users — traders, patients, emergency responders — while the syndicates simply switch to offline methods they used for decades.

The honest fix is narrower and harder: secure the printing presses, rotate question sets, and prosecute the officials who sell them. A society that reaches for a blackout every time it faces malpractice is confessing that it cannot police its own gates. The phone did not break the examination; the gatekeepers did.

content.title: The Water Filter
content.purpose: the correct order of the layers — and what filtering alone cannot do

options.text: between the sand and the gravel
at the very top of the bottle

questions.question: According to the passage, the charcoal layer comes
questions.explanation: Order from the neck upward: cotton wool, then charcoal (“add crushed charcoal”), then sand, then gravel. Charcoal sits directly above the cotton wool.

options.text: makes water clear but not germ-free

questions.question: “Only heat sterilises” means that filtering
questions.explanation: The passage says filtered water “will look clearer, but it is not yet safe” and must be boiled — filtering clarifies appearance; boiling kills germs.

paragraphs: To make a simple water filter, you need a clean plastic bottle, gravel, sand, charcoal, and cotton wool. First, cut off the bottom of the bottle and turn it upside down so the neck points downwards. Place a layer of cotton wool in the neck to stop fine particles escaping, then add crushed charcoal to remove odour and taste. Above the charcoal, pour a thick layer of fine sand, and finish with a layer of gravel to trap the largest impurities.

Pour the dirty water slowly through the wide opening and collect what drips from the neck. The water will look clearer, but it is not yet safe: boiling it for at least five minutes destroys the germs that filtering cannot remove. A filter clarifies; only heat sterilises. Anyone who drinks the filtered water without boiling it has completed only half the task.

content.title: Blue Dusk
content.purpose: the mood of the closing market — and what Alaba takes home

questions.question: The dominant mood of the passage is one of
questions.explanation: Despite the day taking “his money, his patience, and very nearly his temper”, Alaba feels “oddly repaid” and “slightly mended” — loss resolved into calm, not anger or fear.

paragraphs: The market did not close so much as dissolve. Lanterns bloomed one by one above the stalls while the last daylight thinned into a violet haze, and the bargaining — fierce at noon — softened into banter. A woman folded her remaining peppers into a basin with the tenderness of someone putting children to bed, and the scent of roasting corn drifted through the lanes like a rumour.

Alaba lingered at the gate, unwilling to break the spell. The day had taken his money, his patience, and very nearly his temper, yet standing there in the blue dusk he felt oddly repaid. Some places do not merely sell you things, he thought; they return you to yourself, slightly mended.

lessons.title: Summary Writing
lessons.objective: synthesis of ideas from the passages

bullets: One of the five questions on the Section A passage asks for a summary.
A summary restates the main points in your own words, as briefly as the question allows.
It is neither a detail question nor an opinion question.
content.heading: What a summary question asks for
paragraphs: Section A of Use of English gives you a passage of about two hundred words and five questions. One of them asks you to summarise it. The other four are ordinary comprehension questions on the same passage.

A summary question asks you to restate the passage's main points in your own words, as briefly as the question allows. It is not a question about a detail, and it is not an opinion question. It is a test of whether you can tell which parts of a passage carry the weight.

bullets: The instruction gives a number — one sentence, two sentences, ten words. Treat it as a hard limit.
The marks come from: right number of sentences, right length, main point per paragraph, accurate wording.
Writing three sentences when one was asked for is a mark lost for free.
content.heading: What JAMB actually asks you to write
paragraphs: The instruction is usually: 'Summarise the passage in one sentence' or 'in two sentences' or 'in not more than ten words'. The number in the instruction is a hard limit, and JAMB marks against it.

The four marks for a summary question come from four things, roughly: the right number of sentences, the right length, the main point of each paragraph, and accurate wording. Losing a mark for writing three sentences when one was asked for is common and entirely avoidable.

bullets: Mark one phrase per paragraph in the margin — never a quotation.
Find the paragraph that carries the passage; usually the last, but not always.
One sentence per main point, in your own words, in the number you were given.
content.heading: How to build one
paragraphs: Do it in three moves. First, mark the main point of each paragraph in the margin — a single phrase, not a sentence, and never a quotation. Second, look at which paragraph carries the passage. In most passages it is the last one, because the passage usually ends by saying what it has been arguing towards, but not always, and the ones that do not are exactly the ones that catch people.

Third, write. One sentence per main point, using your own words, using the count you were given. If you are writing one sentence, you must cover the whole passage in one sentence, which means a subordinate clause is your friend: the passage is about X, but the writer argues Y.

bullets: Quoting instead of summarising — a summary must be your own words.
Listing every detail instead of dropping what is mentioned in passing.
Adding opinion or outside information — both are marked the same way.
Reporting a character's final quote instead of what the passage is about.
content.heading: What loses marks
paragraphs: Four things lose marks reliably. Quoting the passage instead of summarising it, because a summary must be in your own words. Listing every detail, because a summary drops what the passage mentions in passing. Adding your own opinion, because the summary question is not an opinion question. And adding information the passage does not contain, which is the same mistake as adding opinion and is marked the same way.
There is one more trap. If the passage's last paragraph is a quote from a character, a summary that reports the quote rather than what the passage is about will miss the mark that matters most.

content.body: Count the sentences in your summary before you submit. If the instruction said one sentence and you have written two, cut the less important one. If it said two and you have one, add the paragraph you skipped. Most lost summary marks are counting errors, not comprehension errors.

steps.result: The third paragraph carries it: the market works but may not survive.

content.problem: A three-paragraph passage about a night market: how it grew, why it grew, and an uncertain future because the land is needed for a road. The instruction says: 'Summarise the passage in one sentence.'

hints: Does the sentence say what happened, or does it just say what the passage is about?
The market's growth and the threat to the land are two different things — is either in your sentence?
Rewrite it with the market's situation and its uncertainty, in one sentence.
content.question: Here is a one-sentence summary: 'The passage describes a night market, its traders, its growth and its problems.' Which of the four things that lose marks does this commit, and what would you add to fix it?

content.title: The Return of the Night Market
content.purpose: what the market is, why it grew, and what could end it

options.text: A night market has grown quickly because it is cheap, but its future is uncertain because the land is needed for a road.
The council's road plans are being obstructed by traders who have refused to move.
Traders at the market pay more for space than they would pay for a shop on the main road.
Night markets are a common feature of Nigerian cities and cannot be regulated by councils.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
questions.explanation: A summary must carry the passage's main points in order: the market exists and is large, it grew because it is cheap, and its future is threatened by the road project. B misstates the passage — the council has not been obstructed, the traders have asked for an agreement. C inverts the rent figures. D is a generalisation the passage never makes.

options.text: the landowner who owns the land

questions.question: The daily fee at the market is collected by
questions.explanation: Stated directly, and with a deliberate contrast: 'collected by a rotating committee of traders rather than by the landowner'.

options.text: the number of stalls trading on that Friday
the market's income for the month

questions.question: The figure 214 in paragraph 1 refers to
questions.explanation: 'A count by the market association found 214 stalls trading food, tailoring, phone repairs...' The count is of stalls, and the list that follows are the kinds of trade at those stalls.

options.text: annoyed that something appeared before they had planned for it
amused by the traders who built the market
relieved that the market will move on

questions.question: The phrase 'slightly ruefully' in the last paragraph suggests that the planners are
questions.explanation: 'Ruefully' means with regret. The regret is at being outmanoeuvred: the market 'showed up before they did'. The planners are not amused by the traders — they are rueful that a market arrived without their plan.

options.text: set aside for a particular purpose

questions.question: In paragraph 3, 'earmarked' most nearly means
questions.explanation: 'The land is earmarked for a road project' means the land has been set aside for the road. The context — the council has said so, and the traders have asked for a formal agreement — confirms it.

paragraphs: In the last four years, a night market has appeared on an unused strip of land behind the neighbourhood's old bus depot. It opens at seven in the evening and closes around two in the morning. On a Friday in March, a count by the market association found 214 stalls trading food, tailoring, phone repairs, hairdressing and second-hand clothes.

The market's organisers say its growth has been driven by the cost of rent elsewhere. A trader who paid forty thousand naira a month for a shop on the main road in 2023 pays six thousand for a table at the market. The market charges a small daily fee, which is collected by a rotating committee of traders rather than by the landowner, who has so far declined to sell the land.

Whether it lasts is unclear. The council has said the land is earmarked for a road project, and the traders have asked for a formal agreement. For now the market continues, and the planners have begun referring to it, slightly ruefully, as the thing that showed up before they did.

content.prompt: Take the summary question in The Return of the Night Market. Write your own one-sentence summary now, before you look at the option. Then compare: which of your facts did option A carry that yours missed, and which did yours carry that A left out? An option that is correct is usually slightly longer than a candidate's first attempt — what was missing from yours?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer identifies one specific missing element — usually the uncertainty ('the land is needed for a road') or the cause of the growth ('because it is cheap') — and explains why it matters: without the third paragraph, the summary reports a success story instead of the passage's actual subject, which is a market whose success may be temporary. If your summary was longer than the option, that is not a fault; but if it was longer and still missed the uncertainty, the summary was drifting into detail instead of tracking the passage's argument.

lessons.title: Description Passages
lessons.objective: identify main points/topic sentences in passages

bullets: A description passage has no story and no argument — it makes you see something accurately.
Its topic sentence is the one doing the describing; the rest is detail hanging off it.
Find the topic sentence first and the 'about the whole passage' questions fall before you read the options.
content.heading: What a description passage does
paragraphs: A description passage paints a picture of a person, a place, a thing or a moment. It is not telling you a story and it is not arguing a case. Its whole job is to make you see and feel something accurately, and everything in it — the order of details, the sensory words, the exact size and shape — is chosen to serve that single purpose.

Because the passage has no plot and no argument, its centre of gravity is the topic sentence. That is the sentence doing the describing, and everything after it is detail hanging off that sentence. Find the topic sentence and you have already answered most of the questions about the whole passage before you read a single option.

bullets: Description opens wide and narrows: the whole subject first, then the parts.
It leans on sensory and precise language — colour, texture, temperature, sound, number.
Sequence of events means narration. Signposting words means exposition. Neither means description.
content.heading: How to recognise one
paragraphs: Description passages almost always open with a wide shot and then narrow: the whole thing first, then the parts. The first sentence gives you the subject and its scale — a mound, a market, a particular street — and each following sentence tightens the focus until you are looking at something small and exact.

They also lean hard on sensory language. Not decorative language — precise language. A description will tell you the colour, the texture, the temperature, the sound, the number. If a passage gives you measurements, colours, directions and temperatures, it is a description. If it gives you a sequence of events, it is narration. If it gives you signposting words like first, then, finally and as a result, it is exposition.

bullets: About-the-passage questions answer to the topic sentence or the idea it supports.
Detail questions are stated flatly — scan for the noun in the question.
Inference answers are the option the passage makes more likely without asserting.
content.heading: Where the answers sit
paragraphs: Three question types dominate a description passage, and each has a predictable home.

Questions about the whole passage ask for the main point, and the answer is the topic sentence or the idea it supports. Questions about a part ask for a detail, and the answer is stated flatly somewhere in the paragraph — you find it by scanning for the noun in the question. Inference questions ask for something the passage does not say outright, and the answer is the one option that the passage makes more likely without asserting it.

bullets: One ~200-word passage from some discipline, five questions on it.
The discipline is there to stop you guessing from knowledge instead of reading.
Read once for the topic sentence, once for the details, then answer.
content.heading: How JAMB uses it
paragraphs: JAMB sets one passage of about two hundred words that reflects some discipline — science, history, agriculture, economics — and asks five questions on it. The discipline is there to stop you guessing from prior knowledge and to make you read what is in front of you. That is the trap: candidates who recognise the subject think they know the answer, and then miss the detail the passage actually gives.
Your method should be the same whether or not you know the discipline. Read once for the topic sentence. Read again for the details the questions name. Then answer.

content.body: In a description passage, the first sentence is usually the topic sentence and the last sentence usually carries the writer's attitude. Read those two twice, and the middle once. If you can name the subject from the first line, you already know what every question is about.
