lessons.title: Common Grammar Errors
lessons.objective: Tense, pronoun, and other mistakes that recur in "choose the correct sentence" questions.

content.heading: Common Grammar Errors
paragraphs: Tense, pronoun, and other mistakes that recur in "choose the correct sentence" questions.

bullets: Use the simple past for a completed action with a specific past time: I went to school yesterday (not "I have gone to school yesterday").
Use the present perfect for a past action with present relevance and no definite time: I have finished my revision.
Use the past perfect ("had finished") for the earlier of two actions: By the time I arrived, the lesson had started.
Time markers decide the tense: "two years ago" goes with the simple past; "since" goes with a perfect tense.
In reported speech, shift the tense back: He said he was tired (not "he is tired").
content.heading: Tense errors
paragraphs: Tense questions test whether you can match the verb form to the time marker in the sentence. The time marker usually decides which option is correct.

bullets: After a preposition, use the object form: between you and me (not "you and I").
After "than" and "as", complete the clause mentally: She is taller than I (am).
Use reflexive pronouns only when subject and object are the same person: She dressed herself.
Every pronoun must agree with its antecedent and stay consistent: Everyone should bring their books (informal but common); avoid mixing singular and plural carelessly.
content.heading: Pronoun errors
paragraphs: The choice between "I" and "me" depends on whether the word is doing the action (subject) or receiving it (object). Prepositions always take the object form.

bullets: Double negatives are ungrammatical: "I did not see nothing" → "I did not see anything".
Redundancy: "return back", except "repeat again", "advance forward" — one word carries the idea.
Prepositions: "running for the bus" vs "running to the bus" changes meaning; say "good at", "different from", "prefer … to …", "insist on", "arrive at/in".
Quantifiers: "much" for uncountable (much water), "many" for plural countable (many books); "fewer" for countable, "less" for uncountable.
Confusables: its/it’s, whose/who’s, there/their/they’re, affect/effect, borrow/lend, advice/advise.
Dangling modifier: "Walking to school, the bell rang" — the person walked, not the bell. Attach the modifier to the right subject.
content.heading: Errors examiners repeat
paragraphs: A small set of errors appears again and again in "choose the correct sentence" questions. Learn these and you eliminate most wrong options at once.

content.body: Read each option word-for-word. Most "best sentence" questions test one rule, so a single wrong word (have/went, their/its, me/I) tells you the answer.
content.title: Exam tip

pair: The list of items are on the desk.
The list of items is on the desk.
content.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun (list), not with the noun nearest to it (items). Ignore prepositional phrases when finding the subject.
content.counterexample: The list of items is on the desk — but: The items on the desk are mine.

pair: Neither the teacher nor the students was present.
Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
content.rule: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — students, so were.
content.counterexample: Neither the students nor the teacher was present. (Nearer subject: teacher → was.)

pair: He requested for permission to leave.
He requested permission to leave.
content.rule: Request is transitive here — it takes the object directly. “Request for” only appears in the noun phrase “a request for…”.
content.counterexample: She applied for the job (apply needs for), but: She requested an extension (request takes none).

pair: The reason he left is because he was tired.
The reason he left is that he was tired.
content.rule: “The reason is…” must be completed with a that-clause, not a because-clause — because already contains the reason, so the sentence repeats itself.
content.counterexample: The reason is that the road flooded — never “the reason is because…”.

content.rule: The relative pronoun already stands for the boy — adding “him” gives the clause two objects. One slot, one pronoun.
content.answer: The boy whom the teacher praised passed the examination. (Accept: The boy who was praised by the teacher passed.)
content.prompt: Rebuild this into one correct sentence: “The boy who the teacher praised him passed the examination.”

content.rule: Hardly/scarcely at the front forces inversion — auxiliary verb before the subject. No inversion, no mark.
content.answer: Hardly had the referee blown the whistle when the crowd rushed onto the pitch.
content.prompt: Rebuild this into one correct sentence: “Hardly the referee had blown the whistle when the crowd rushed onto the pitch.”
Which of the four pairs above would still catch you under time pressure — and what one-second check will you run on every underlining that looks like it?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names the specific trap (“neither…nor distance agreement”), states the check as a physical habit (“cover the phrase between the subject and the verb, then re-read”), and gives the counterexample from memory. That check is your insurance policy on Saturday.

pair: She plays piano very well.
She plays the piano very well.
content.rule: Instruments take the definite article: play the piano, the guitar, the drums. Drop it only for the activity in general (“Piano is fun”).
content.counterexample: He plays the guitar — but: Guitar music filled the hall (general, no article).

pair: The meeting is on Monday morning at 10 o’clock.
The meeting is in Monday morning at 10 o’clock.
content.rule: Time ladder: at for clock times (at 10), on for days and dated mornings (on Monday, on Monday morning), in for months/years/periods (in June, in the morning).
content.counterexample: On Monday morning at 10 — never “in Monday”. But: in the morning (no day named).

pair: She said she will come tomorrow.
She said she would come the next day.
content.rule: Reported speech steps the tense back: will → would, and the time marker shifts (tomorrow → the next day). The reporting verb “said” is past, so the whole clause follows it.
content.counterexample: She says she will come tomorrow (present reporting verb — no shift). She said she would come.

pair: The principal suggested that he goes home.
The principal suggested that he go home.
content.rule: Suggest, insist, demand, recommend take the base form (subjunctive): no -s, no tense. “Suggested that he go”, never “goes” or “went”.
content.counterexample: They insisted that she stay — never “stays”. Test with: The rule demands it be so (not “is”).

pair: Walking home, the rain started suddenly.
Walking home, I was caught by sudden rain.
content.rule: An opening -ing phrase must describe the subject that follows. Rain cannot walk — attach the phrase to the walker (I), or the sentence dangles.
content.counterexample: Exhausted, the team slept (team can be exhausted ✓). Exhausted, the whistle blew (whistle cannot ✗).

pair: You are coming with us, isn’t it?
You are coming with us, aren’t you?
content.rule: Question tags echo the statement’s auxiliary and subject: are + you → aren’t you. “Isn’t it” answers nothing in this sentence — it is the tag of last resort, not a universal one.
content.counterexample: She can swim, can’t she? They left early, didn’t they? (Match auxiliary + pronoun every time.)

lessons.title: Parts of Speech
lessons.objective: The eight word classes every English question depends on — and how to spot them in a sentence.

content.heading: Parts of Speech
paragraphs: The eight word classes every English question depends on — and how to spot them in a sentence.

bullets: A noun names something: a person (student), a place (library), a thing (calculator), or an idea (freedom). Common nouns are general; proper nouns are specific and capitalised (University of Ilorin).
A pronoun stands in for a noun: I, you, he, she, it, we, they, who, which. It must agree with the noun it replaces.
A verb expresses action or a state of being: run, think, is, was, have. Every sentence needs at least one.
An adjective modifies a noun: a brilliant answer, a quick revision.
An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb: ran quickly, quite good, very quickly.
A preposition shows position or relationship: in, on, at, under, between, after.
A conjunction joins words or clauses: and, but, or, because, although.
An interjection is a short exclamation: Wow! Oh! Ouch!
content.heading: The eight parts of speech
paragraphs: Every English sentence is built from eight kinds of words, called parts of speech. Each one has a job. If you can name the job a word is doing, you can answer most "identify the part of speech" questions quickly.

bullets: Decide the class by position and function in the sentence, not by memory.
"The" before a noun is an article; before an adjective it can turn the adjective into a noun — "the rich" means rich people.
content.heading: Words that change class
paragraphs: The same word can belong to more than one class, depending on the job it does in the sentence. Do not memorise a list of words; instead, ask what the word is doing where it sits.
Example: "Fast" is an adjective in "a fast car" but an adverb in "drives fast". "Run" is a verb in "I run daily" but a noun in "a quick run".

bullets: Do not call "the" an adjective; examiners classify it as an article (or determiner).
Possessive adjectives (my, your, our) must be followed by a noun: "my book", never "I book".
A full sentence needs a finite verb — one marked for tense — not just a participle.
Adverbs of frequency (always, often, rarely) go before the main verb but after "am/is/are": He is always late.
content.heading: Exam traps
paragraphs: Examiners set traps with words that look like one class but belong to another. Learn these three common ones and you dodge the worst of them.

content.body: When asked to identify a part of speech, ask one question about the word: does it name (noun), replace a name (pronoun), show action (verb), or modify (adjective/adverb)? That is usually enough.
content.title: Exam tip

lessons.title: Mood, Tense and Aspect
lessons.objective: Distinguish tense, aspect and mood, and choose the correct verb form for time, completion and attitude.

content.heading: Mood, tense and aspect
paragraphs: A student writes 'I am living here since 2019' and loses the mark, because the sentence needs a tense and an aspect that agree with 'since'.

content.heading: Tense and aspect together
paragraphs: Tense locates the action in past, present or future. Aspect describes it: simple for a fact, continuous for progress, and perfect for completion with relevance to a later time.

The combinations give forms such as 'she writes' for a habit, 'she is writing' for now, 'she has written' for a finished action with present relevance, and 'she has been writing' for an action continuing up to now.
'Since' and 'for' with a present result take the present perfect: 'I have lived here since 2019', not 'I am living here since 2019'. 'For' names a length of time; 'since' names a starting point.
bullets: Tense tells you when.
Aspect tells you finished or continuing.
Since takes a point in time; for takes a length.
content.takeaway: Tense gives the time; aspect gives the shape of the action.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
check.why: A situation that began in the past and continues now takes the present perfect, and 'since' marks the starting point.

content.heading: Progressive and perfect
paragraphs: The progressive (be + -ing) presents an action in progress; the perfect (have + past participle) presents it as complete before a reference point. 'She was cooking when I arrived' sets one action inside another.
Stative verbs such as know, believe, own, belong and seem resist the progressive. Say 'I know the answer', not 'I am knowing the answer'.
The past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions: 'By the time we arrived, the bus had left.' The future perfect does the same for a future reference point: 'By June, she will have finished'.
bullets: Progressive: the action is in progress.
Perfect: the action is complete before a reference point.
Stative verbs avoid the progressive.
content.takeaway: Use the perfect when one action must be finished before another.

check.question: By the time we arrived, the bus ______.
check.why: The bus left before our arrival, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect.

visual.caption: Tense fixes the time; aspect fixes whether the action is finished or still unfolding.

content.heading: Mood
paragraphs: Mood shows the speaker's attitude to the action. The indicative states a fact, the imperative gives a command, and the subjunctive expresses a wish, a demand or a hypothetical.
The subjunctive keeps the base verb after expressions such as 'it is essential that', 'I recommend that' and 'if I were': 'It is essential that he go early' and 'If I were you, I would wait'.
The imperative has no subject and no tense: 'Sit down' and 'Do not enter'. Questions use the interrogative: 'Has she left?' The exam often tests 'If I were' against the incorrect 'If I was'.
bullets: Indicative: a fact.
Imperative: a command.
Subjunctive: a wish, demand or hypothesis.
content.takeaway: Mood tells you whether the speaker states, commands or imagines.

check.question: If I ______ you, I would apologise.
check.why: A hypothetical condition takes the subjunctive 'were', even with a singular subject.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Tense is not the same as aspect. 'She wrote' and 'She has written' are both past-related, but only the second links the action to now.

content.problem: By next June, Ada ______ here for five years. Choose the correct form: will live, will have lived, lives or lived.

steps.reason: 'By next June' points to a moment in the future.
steps.result: The sentence needs a future form.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the five-year period complete at that moment?

steps.reason: 'For five years' measures a period completed by the reference point.
steps.result: The action will be complete by next June, so the future perfect fits.

steps.reason: The future perfect is will + have + past participle.
steps.result: Ada will have lived here for five years.

content.question: I wish I ______ the answer yesterday. Choose: know, knew, had known or have known.
hints: The wish is about a past event that cannot be changed.
A past regret takes the past perfect after 'wish'.
The correct form is had known.

lessons.title: Concord Rules
lessons.objective: The rules of agreement between subject and verb — a heavily tested area of Nigerian English exams.

content.heading: Concord Rules
paragraphs: The rules of agreement between subject and verb — a heavily tested area of Nigerian English exams.

bullets: A singular subject takes a singular verb: The student studies. (add –s to the verb in the present tense)
A plural subject takes a plural verb: The students study.
Words between the subject and verb do not decide the verb: The box of matches is on the shelf. ("box" governs the verb, not "matches")
content.heading: Core subject–verb agreement
paragraphs: Concord means agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. In the present tense this usually just means adding or removing an –s.

bullets: Each, every, everyone, everybody, anybody, nobody, nothing take a singular verb: Everybody is here.
Neither and either are singular: Neither of the answers is correct.
With "either … or" and "neither … nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
Both (of them) takes a plural verb: Both of the students were present.
Collective nouns (committee, team, family) are usually treated as singular: The committee has given its report.
"The number of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" takes a plural: The number of students has risen. A number of students are absent.
content.heading: Subjects that fool candidates
paragraphs: Some subjects look plural but behave as singular, and some quantifier phrases switch the verb. These are the most-tested patterns, so learn the list.

bullets: Amounts, distances and periods of time are singular: Ten years is a long time.
With fractions and percentages, the verb matches the noun after "of": Half of the cake has gone; half of the students have gone.
"News" looks plural but takes a singular verb: The news is good.
"The police" takes a plural verb: The police are investigating.
"There is/are" decides by the subject that follows: There are many questions left.
content.heading: Quantities, time and distance
paragraphs: Amounts confuse candidates because they look plural. The rule is simple: a sum, distance or period treated as one unit is singular.

content.body: To settle a concord question, cross out every clause between the head noun and the verb. Then match the verb to the remaining head word.
content.title: Exam tip

lessons.title: Degrees of Comparison
lessons.objective: Form the positive, comparative and superlative degrees correctly, and choose the degree and marker that match the number of items compared.

content.heading: Degrees of comparison
paragraphs: A shopper says one phone is 'more cheaper' than another and the sentence collapses. Comparison runs on a small set of forms, and the exam checks whether you can pick the right one.

content.heading: Three degrees, three forms
paragraphs: The positive degree names a quality without comparing: 'This bag is heavy.' The comparative compares two things: 'This bag is heavier than that one.' The superlative sets one item above a group of three or more: 'This is the heaviest bag in the shop.'

Formation follows syllable count. One-syllable adjectives add -er and -est (cheap, cheaper, cheapest), while adjectives of three or more syllables use more and most (expensive, more expensive, most expensive).

Two-syllable adjectives vary: happy becomes happier, but careful becomes more careful. Spelling changes apply before the ending: y turns to i in heavier, the consonant doubles in bigger, and the silent e drops in larger. Learn the spelling alongside the form.
bullets: Positive: no comparison at all.
Comparative: exactly two items.
Superlative: three or more items.
content.takeaway: The degree tells you how many things are being compared.

check.question: Which is the superlative form of 'useful'?
check.why: 'Useful' has two syllables and takes 'most' for the superlative; 'usefullest' is not an English form.

content.heading: Comparing like with like
paragraphs: Use the comparative for two items and the superlative for three or more. 'She is taller than her sister' compares two people, while 'She is the tallest of the three sisters' compares three.

The markers differ. The comparative takes 'than'; the superlative takes 'the' and usually 'of' or 'in': 'the best of the three', 'the fastest in the class'. A comparative without 'than' is often incomplete, and a superlative without 'the' is often wrong.

Never double the marker. 'More better', 'most tallest' and 'more easier' are wrong because the form already carries the comparison. Compare like with like as well: say 'Lagos is bigger than Ibadan', not 'Lagos is bigger than Ibadan's population'.
bullets: Comparative: two items, followed by 'than'.
Superlative: three or more, preceded by 'the'.
Never combine 'more' with -er or 'most' with -est.
content.takeaway: Count the items first, then choose the form and its marker.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is more taller than her sister.
She is the tallest of the two sisters.
She is taller than her sister.
She is tallest than her sister.
check.why: Two people take the comparative 'taller' with 'than'; 'more taller' doubles the marker and 'tallest' is superlative.

visual.caption: The number of items decides both the form and the marker that follows it.

content.heading: Irregulars and fixed patterns
paragraphs: Some adjectives do not take -er or -est at all: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further, furthest; little, less, least; many and much, more, most. There is no rule that generates these, so learn each set whole.
Several patterns are fixed. 'As tall as' states equality, 'not so tall as' states inequality, and 'the more you practise, the better you become' links two changes that rise together.

Watch the near misses. 'Elder' describes family order and never takes 'than', while 'older' is the general comparative; 'lesser' means smaller in importance, not size. 'Farther' is usual for physical distance, while 'further' covers distance or addition.
bullets: Good, better, best; bad, worse, worst.
'As ... as' states equality.
'Elder' takes no 'than'; 'older' does.
content.takeaway: Learn the irregulars as whole sets, because no rule will generate them.

check.question: The ______ of the two routes is the one through town.
check.why: Two routes take the comparative 'shorter'; 'shortest' would need three or more routes.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: 'More' and '-er' never work together. If the adjective already ends in -er, the comparison is complete.

content.problem: Choose the correct form: 'This is the (good) result of the three tests.'

steps.reason: The degree depends on how many things are compared.
steps.result: Three tests are being compared.
steps.predictPrompt: Which degree handles three or more?

steps.operation: Check whether the adjective is regular
steps.reason: Irregular adjectives do not take -er or -est.
steps.result: 'Good' is irregular: good, better, best.

steps.reason: A superlative normally takes 'the'.
steps.result: This is the best result of the three tests.

content.question: Complete each sentence: 'She is the ______ (intelligent) girl in the class' and 'My bag is ______ (heavy) than yours.'
hints: Count the items in each sentence.
The class has more than two girls.
Two bags take the comparative.

lessons.title: Question Tags
lessons.objective: Add the correct question tag by repeating the statement's auxiliary and tense, reversing polarity and replacing the subject with a pronoun.

content.heading: Question tags
paragraphs: A speaker says 'You are coming, aren't you?' and waits for a nod. The short tail turns a statement into a check, and its form follows rules rather than intonation.

content.heading: The tag mirrors the statement
paragraphs: A question tag is a short question added to a statement. It repeats the auxiliary and subject of that statement, and it reverses the polarity: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag.
'She is ready, isn't she?' is positive then negative. 'She isn't ready, is she?' is negative then positive. The subject becomes a pronoun: 'Musa is late, isn't he?' rather than 'isn't Musa?'.

The tag agrees in tense and person. 'They went home, didn't they?' keeps the past tense, and 'We can swim, can't we?' keeps the modal. A mismatch in auxiliary, tense or pronoun is the commonest error in this item type.
bullets: Reverse the polarity of the statement.
Repeat its auxiliary and tense.
Replace the subject with a pronoun.
content.takeaway: The tag repeats the statement and reverses its polarity.

check.question: Bola is coming, ______?
check.why: The statement is positive and uses 'is', so the tag is negative and keeps 'is' with the pronoun 'she'.

content.heading: Finding the auxiliary
paragraphs: When the statement already has an auxiliary, the tag uses it: is, are, was, were, have, has, had, will, would, can, could, may, might, must or should. 'They have finished, haven't they?' repeats 'have'.
When there is no auxiliary, the tag supplies do, does or did to match the tense: 'She sings well, doesn't she?', 'They left early, didn't they?' and 'You like tea, don't you?'.

Be careful with 'have'. As a main verb meaning possess, it can take do: 'You have a car, don't you?' As an auxiliary it repeats itself: 'You have seen it, haven't you?'. The same split applies to 'be' and 'do'.
bullets: Repeat an auxiliary if one is present.
Supply do, does or did if there is none.
'Have' as a main verb takes 'do'.
content.takeaway: If the statement has no auxiliary, build one with do, does or did.

check.question: They arrived late, ______?
check.why: The statement is positive and has no auxiliary, so the tag uses the past tense 'did' with 'n't' and the pronoun 'they'.

visual.caption: Build a tag by working through the statement in four moves.

content.heading: Special cases
paragraphs: Some tags do not follow the ordinary pattern. After 'let's' use 'shall we?', after an imperative use 'will you?' or 'won't you?', and after 'I am' standard British English uses 'aren't I?'.

Indefinite subjects take a plural pronoun: 'Everybody has arrived, haven't they?' and 'Nobody called, did they?'. 'Nothing' takes 'it': 'Nothing happened, did it?'. These pronouns follow meaning rather than grammatical number.

Negative adverbs change the polarity. Never, hardly, scarcely, barely and no one make the statement negative, so the tag is positive: 'He never smiles, does he?'. A statement with 'used to' takes 'didn't': 'She used to live here, didn't she?'.
bullets: 'Let's' takes 'shall we?'.
Imperatives take 'will you?'.
Negative adverbs force a positive tag.
content.takeaway: Special subjects and negative adverbs overturn the ordinary pattern.

check.question: Let's go now, ______?
check.why: 'Let's' is a fixed exception: it always takes 'shall we?' regardless of the ordinary polarity rule.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Say the statement and the tag aloud. If the two halves have the same polarity, the tag is wrong.

content.problem: Add the correct tag: 'The students had left before noon.'

steps.reason: The tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement.
steps.result: The auxiliary is 'had'.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the statement positive or negative?

steps.reason: A positive statement takes a negative tag.
steps.result: The tag begins 'hadn't'.

steps.reason: The subject must become a pronoun that matches in person and number.
steps.result: 'The students' becomes 'they', so the tag is 'hadn't they?'.

content.question: Add tags to these sentences: 'Nobody phoned, ______?' and 'You have eaten, ______?'
hints: 'Nobody' is negative, so the tag turns positive.
The subject 'nobody' takes 'they'.
'Have' here is an auxiliary, so it repeats.

lessons.title: Mechanics: Spelling and Punctuation
lessons.objective: Apply the spelling conventions and punctuation marks JAMB tests, including suffix rules, apostrophes, semicolons and confusable words.

content.heading: Mechanics
paragraphs: A candidate writes 'The dogs tail wagged' and loses a mark for a missing apostrophe. Mechanics is the set of small marks and spellings that carry meaning, and the exam tests them directly.

content.heading: Spelling rules that hold
paragraphs: Use i before e except after c, when the sound is long /iː/: believe, chief, receive and ceiling. The rule has exceptions such as seize, weird and either, so learn those words separately instead of trusting the rhyme everywhere.

Double the final consonant when a one-syllable word ending in one vowel plus one consonant takes a suffix beginning with a vowel: big becomes bigger, stop becomes stopped, run becomes running. Do not double when the stress is not on the last syllable: visit becomes visited, not 'visitted'.

Drop a silent e before a vowel suffix (make becomes making) but keep it before a consonant suffix (hope becomes hopeful). Change y to i after a consonant (carry becomes carried) but keep it after a vowel (play becomes played).
bullets: I before e except after c, with exceptions.
Double after a short stressed vowel.
Drop silent e before a vowel suffix.
content.takeaway: Spelling rules work by sound and stress, not by memorising each word alone.

check.question: Which spelling is correct?
check.why: After c the order reverses to ei, so the correct spelling is 'receive'.

content.heading: Punctuation that changes meaning
paragraphs: An apostrophe shows possession or marks a contraction. 'The boy's book' is one boy's book, 'the boys' books' is several boys' books, and 'it's' means 'it is' while 'its' shows possession.

A comma separates items and marks off extra information: 'After the meeting, we ate.' A semicolon joins two closely related clauses: 'The rain stopped; we continued.' A colon introduces a list or an explanation.

A hyphen joins the parts of a compound word (well-known, mother-in-law), while a dash marks a break in thought. Using one for the other is a common exam error, so check whether the mark is joining or interrupting.
bullets: Apostrophe: possession or contraction.
Semicolon joins related clauses.
Hyphen joins; dash interrupts.
content.takeaway: Each mark has one job, and swapping them changes the sentence.

check.question: Which is the correct plural possessive?
check.why: 'Children' is already plural and does not end in s, so the possessive adds 's: children's.

visual.caption: The same apostrophe does two different jobs, and the test tells them apart.

content.heading: Confusable words and capitals
paragraphs: Many errors come from words that sound alike. 'Its' is possessive and 'it's' is 'it is'; 'whose' is possessive and 'who's' is 'who is'; 'their' is possessive, 'there' is a place and 'they're' is 'they are'.

Other pairs differ in meaning: affect is a verb and effect is a noun; principal means head or main and principle means a rule; complement completes and compliment praises; stationary means still and stationery means paper.

Capitalise proper nouns, the first word of a sentence, days, months and nationalities, but not the seasons. Write 'Nigeria', 'Nigerian', 'Monday' and 'January', but 'summer'. Titles take capitals only when they precede a name.
bullets: Its is possessive; it's means 'it is'.
Affect is the verb; effect is the noun.
Capitalise proper nouns, not seasons.
content.takeaway: Test a confusable word by expanding the contraction or substituting a synonym.

check.question: The new rule will ______ everyone.
check.why: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence; after 'will' the base form is needed, and 'effect' is normally a noun.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A missing apostrophe can reverse a meaning: 'the girls' bags' and 'the girl's bags' describe different owners.

content.problem: Correct the sentence: 'Its raining, so the childrens books are wet.'

steps.reason: 'Its' without an apostrophe is possessive, but the sentence needs 'it is'.
steps.result: 'Its' becomes 'It's'.
steps.predictPrompt: Which noun owns the books?

steps.reason: 'Children' is an irregular plural that does not end in s.
steps.result: The possessive is 'children's'.

steps.reason: Both marks must now carry the right meaning.
steps.result: 'It's raining, so the children's books are wet.'

content.question: Choose the correct word in each pair: 'The medicine had no (effect / affect)' and '(Whose / Who's) bag is this?'
hints: One word is a noun, the other a verb.
The second sentence means 'who owns'.
'Effect' is the noun; 'whose' is the possessive.

lessons.title: Vocabulary & Idioms
lessons.objective: Crack synonyms, antonyms, word-in-context and the idioms that recur in Nigerian exams.

content.heading: Vocabulary & Idioms
paragraphs: Crack synonyms, antonyms, word-in-context and the idioms that recur in Nigerian exams.

bullets: Read two or three lines around the word before you choose.
Watch for a definition packed into the same sentence: "a remedy — a cure".
Use restatement and examples: "facilitate, that is, ease" or "for instance, …".
Look for contrast words — however, but, although — they signal the opposite meaning.
content.heading: Finding a word’s meaning from context
paragraphs: You are rarely expected to know every word. Instead, the passage around the word gives the clues. Read a little wider than the one line before choosing.

bullets: Reduce the target word to a simple everyday synonym, then match from the options.
Ignore similar sounds: synonyms must match in meaning, not in rhythm.
Use prefixes: un-, in-, im-, dis-, non- mean "not" (unclear, impossible); re- means "again" (rewrite); pre- means "before".
Suffixes show the word class: –ion, –ment; –y; –able (adjectives) usually form nouns; –ly forms adverbs.
content.heading: Synonyms and antonyms
paragraphs: For synonym questions, reduce the target word to a simple everyday equivalent, then match it to the options. For antonyms, think of the everyday opposite first.

bullets: By and large = on the whole. In the long run = eventually. Take for granted = accept without appreciating. Put up with = tolerate.
Call off = cancel. Carry out = perform. Look into = investigate. Run into = meet by chance.
Break the ice = start a conversation. Spill the beans = reveal a secret. Once in a blue moon = very rarely.
A blessing in disguise = a hidden good from a seemingly bad situation. Out of the blue = unexpectedly. Behind the times = old-fashioned.
Idioms are fixed: do not rearrange their words; we say "under no circumstances", not "in no circumstances".
content.heading: Idioms and phrasal verbs to know
paragraphs: Idioms are fixed phrases whose meaning is different from the literal words. Learn them as blocks, not as single words.

content.body: When two options seem equally good, choose the more idiomatic or more formal one. The wrong options are usually plausible-sounding but slightly misused.

lessons.title: Vowels: Monothongs, Diphthongs and Triphthongs
lessons.objective: Distinguish monophthongs, diphthongs and triphthongs by the number of vowel qualities a speaker glides through.

content.heading: Vowel sounds
paragraphs: A speaker saying 'sit' holds one vowel quality, but in 'sight' the tongue moves from one quality to another. That movement separates the vowel types JAMB asks about.

content.heading: One steady sound or a glide
paragraphs: A monophthong is one steady vowel sound. RP has twelve, including /iː/ in seat, /ɪ/ in sit, /æ/ in cat and /ɜː/ in bird. Five are long (/iː/, /ɑː/, /ɔː/, /uː/, /ɜː/) and the rest are short.

A diphthong glides from one vowel quality to another. It has eight members, such as /eɪ/ in bay, /aɪ/ in buy and /ɔɪ/ in boy. The schwa /ə/ is the weak vowel of unstressed syllables, as in the second syllable of 'sofa'.
A triphthong glides through three qualities, as in player /eɪə/ and fire /aɪə/. It is a diphthong followed by a schwa.
bullets: Monophthong: one steady quality.
Diphthong: a glide between two qualities.
Triphthong: a glide through three qualities.
content.takeaway: Count the vowel qualities you hear, not the vowel letters you see.

check.question: Which word contains a diphthong?
check.why: /aɪ/ moves from one quality towards another; the other three hold a single vowel throughout.

visual.caption: A monophthong stays put; a diphthong moves, whatever the spelling suggests.

rows.right: Often a, e, i or o plus y or w
The tongue moves during the sound

content.heading: Telling vowels apart in the exam
paragraphs: Two candidates may hear 'ship' and 'sheep' as the same word, yet the exam treats their vowels as different. Length and tongue position carry the distinction.

Minimal pairs expose it: ship /ɪ/ against sheep /iː/, bad /æ/ against bard /ɑː/, cot /ɒ/ against caught /ɔː/, and full /ʊ/ against fool /uː/. Length and tongue position separate each pair, not the spelling.

Spelling misleads. 'Bread' has one vowel sound /e/ despite two vowel letters, 'my' has the diphthong /aɪ/ despite one letter, and 'queue' is /kjuː/. Say the word aloud before you decide which sound it contains.
bullets: Use minimal pairs, not spelling.
Long and short vowels are different sounds.
Nigerian English may merge pairs the exam keeps apart.
content.takeaway: The exam tests sounds, and spelling is only a clue.

check.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'bird'?
check.why: Bird and burn both carry /ɜː/; bead has /iː/, bed has /e/ and bard has /ɑː/.

content.heading: Triphthongs and the traps
paragraphs: A triphthong appears where a diphthong is followed by /ə/: fire /faɪə/, our /aʊə/, player /pleɪə/, loyal /lɔɪə/ and lower /ləʊə/. Spelling gives no reliable signal, because the same letters can spell a monophthong in another word.

In fast connected speech the glide is often smoothed, so 'fire' may sound like one long syllable rather than three qualities. Exam items usually ask about the underlying sound, not the smoothed version.

The commonest error is counting letters. 'Beautiful' begins with /bjuː/, a consonant plus a vowel, while 'beauty' contains /juː/; neither is a triphthong just because it has many letters. Listen for the number of qualities, then label the sound.
bullets: Triphthong: a diphthong plus schwa.
Examples: fire, our, player.
Ignore spelling and letter count.
content.takeaway: A triphthong is three vowel qualities in one syllable, often smoothed in speech.

check.question: Which word contains a triphthong?
check.why: Buyer glides through /aɪə/; bay and boat are diphthongs and bit is a monophthong.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Vowel letters are not vowel sounds. 'Food' has two letters but one sound; 'my' has one letter but two qualities.

content.problem: Which word contains a diphthong: seat, sit, sight or set?

steps.reason: The vowel is the part that carries the syllable.
steps.result: All four are one-syllable words with one vowel each.
steps.predictPrompt: Now listen for movement inside that vowel.

steps.reason: A diphthong changes quality within the same syllable.
steps.result: Sight moves from /a/ towards /ɪ/; the other three stay steady.

steps.reason: The question asks for a diphthong, not merely a long vowel.
steps.result: Sight /saɪt/ is the answer.

content.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'caught': cot, coat, court or cut?
hints: Say 'caught' and hold the vowel.
It is the long open back vowel /ɔː/.
Cot has /ɒ/, coat has /əʊ/, cut has /ʌ/.

lessons.title: Consonants and Consonant Clusters
lessons.objective: Classify consonant sounds by voicing, place and manner, and count the sounds in clusters rather than the letters.

content.heading: Consonant sounds
paragraphs: Put two fingers on your throat and say 'pat', then 'bat'. The first leaves the throat still; the second buzzes.

content.heading: Voiced or voiceless
paragraphs: That buzz is voicing, the first division of English consonants. Pairs such as /p/–/b/, /t/–/d/, /k/–/g/, /f/–/v/, /s/–/z/ and /θ/–/ð/ differ only in voicing.

RP has twenty-four consonant sounds. Eight are voiceless: /p t k f θ s ʃ tʃ/; the rest are voiced, including all nasals and /l r w j/. All vowels are voiced, so the question applies only to consonants.

Exam items ask which sound appears in a word, so say the word and isolate the sound. 'Think' begins with the voiceless /θ/, while 'this' begins with its voiced partner /ð/. Voicing can also change with a suffix: the -s in cats is /s/, but in dogs it is /z/.
bullets: Voicing is vibration of the vocal cords.
Voiceless and voiced sounds form pairs.
Isolate the sound, not the letter.
content.takeaway: If the throat buzzes, the consonant is voiced.

check.question: Which word begins with a voiceless sound?
check.why: Think begins with /θ/, which has no voicing; bat, this and judge all begin with voiced sounds.

visual.caption: Each pair uses the same mouth position; only voicing changes.

content.heading: Place and manner
paragraphs: Where the airflow is blocked gives the place: lips for /p b m/, lip and teeth for /f v/, teeth for /θ ð/, the ridge behind the teeth for /t d s z n l/, and the soft palate for /k g ŋ/.

How it is released gives the manner: plosives stop and release (/p t k/), fricatives force air through a narrow gap (/f s ʃ/), affricates stop then release slowly (/tʃ dʒ/), nasals pass through the nose (/m n ŋ/), and approximants barely obstruct (/r w j/).

The labels combine. /tʃ/ in church is a voiceless palato-alveolar affricate, and /ŋ/ at the end of sing is a voiced velar nasal. Every consonant has one place and one manner, so a full answer names both.
bullets: Place: lips, teeth, ridge, palate.
Manner: plosive, fricative, affricate, nasal.
Combine both labels for the full name.
content.takeaway: Name a consonant by voicing, place and manner together.

check.question: The first sound in 'judge' is ______.
check.why: /dʒ/ stops the airflow and releases it slowly, and the vocal cords vibrate, so it is a voiced affricate.

content.heading: Clusters
paragraphs: A cluster is two or more consonants with no vowel between them. English allows three at the start, as in street /str/, spring /spr/ and scream /skr/, and up to four at the end.

Nigerian English often breaks a cluster by inserting a vowel ('sitreet') or drops one of its sounds ('tes' for tests). Both change the syllable count and can cost marks, so practise the cluster without an inserted vowel.

Count sounds, not letters. 'Box' is /bɒks/, four sounds; 'thought' is /θɔːt/, three; 'strengths' is /streŋθs/, seven sounds, six of them consonants. Clusters can cross a syllable boundary in connected speech, but exam items usually test them inside one word.
bullets: No vowel sits inside a cluster.
Initial /str/, /spr/, /skr/; final /-sts/, /-sks/.
Count sounds, not letters.
content.takeaway: A cluster is consonants touching, with no vowel to separate them.

check.question: How many consonant sounds are in 'strengths'?
check.why: The sounds are /s t r e ŋ θ s/: six consonants around the single vowel /e/.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The letter x usually spells two sounds: /ks/ in box and /gz/ in exam. Count the sounds, not the letters.

content.problem: How many consonant sounds are in the word 'strengths'?

steps.reason: The syllable must be heard before it can be counted.
steps.result: Strengths is one syllable: /streŋθs/.
steps.predictPrompt: Which sounds are vowels?

steps.reason: Each distinct sound counts once, even when several letters spell it.
steps.result: The sounds are /s/, /t/, /r/, /e/, /ŋ/, /θ/ and /s/.

steps.reason: Remove the vowel /e/ and count what remains.
steps.result: Six consonants: s, t, r, ŋ, θ, s.

content.question: Which word begins with /dʒ/: gin, game, gain or gone?
hints: Say each word and listen to the first sound.
Game, gain and gone begin with the voiced plosive /g/.
Gin begins with the voiced affricate /dʒ/.

lessons.title: Rhymes and Homophones
lessons.objective: Identify rhyme by the stressed vowel and following sounds, and distinguish homophones from near misses and homographs.

content.heading: Rhyme and homophones
paragraphs: A poet pairs 'moon' with 'June' and the ear accepts it, but 'moon' and 'book' do not rhyme. The difference is where the sound match begins.

content.heading: How rhyme works
paragraphs: A rhyme repeats the stressed vowel and every sound after it, while the sound before it changes. Cat and hat rhyme; cat and cap do not, because the final consonant differs.
The match starts at the stressed syllable, so nation and station rhyme on '-ation', and belief and relief rhyme on '-lief'. The sound before the stressed vowel is free to differ.

Words with the same ending letters do not always rhyme: love and move share no vowel sound, and food and good differ in vowel length. Rhyme is also not identity: a word does not rhyme with itself, and repeated sounds at the start of words are alliteration, not rhyme.
bullets: Rhyme starts at the stressed vowel.
Everything after it must match.
Spelling is not a guide.
content.takeaway: Rhyme is a sound match from the stressed vowel to the end.

check.question: Which word rhymes with 'though'?
check.why: Though and toe both end in /əʊ/; cow ends in /aʊ/, tough in /ʌf/ and through in /uː/.

visual.caption: Rhyme matches an ending; a homophone matches the whole word.

content.heading: Homophones
paragraphs: Homophones sound alike but are spelled differently and mean different things: sea and see, meat and meet, peace and piece, right and write, their and there. Some sets have three spellings, as in their, there and they're, where the apostrophe marks a contraction.
Homographs are the opposite trap: one spelling with different sounds or meanings, such as lead /liːd/ and lead /led/, or bow /bəʊ/ and bow /baʊ/.
The exam may ask which pair are homophones, or which word sounds like a given word. Test the pronunciation first, then check that the meanings differ.
bullets: Same sound, different spelling and meaning.
Homographs: same spelling, different sound or meaning.
Pronounce before choosing.
content.takeaway: Homophones agree in sound and disagree in spelling and sense.

check.question: Which pair are homophones?
check.why: Write and right are both /raɪt/; the other pairs differ in voicing or vowel sound.

content.heading: Near misses
paragraphs: Many pairs look like homophones but differ in one sound. Loose /luːs/ and lose /luːz/ differ in voicing; advice /ədˈvaɪs/ and advise /ədˈvaɪz/ do the same. Voicing is the commonest single-sound difference: /s/ against /z/, /f/ against /v/, and /θ/ against /ð/.
Rhyme traps work the same way: food /uː/ does not rhyme with good /ʊ/, and cloth /θ/ does not rhyme with clothe /ð/. Vowel length and final voicing decide most of these near misses.
Nigerian English sometimes merges hear and here, or keeps apart pairs that standard English joins. The exam follows the standard, so learn the contrast rather than your own habit.
bullets: Check voicing: /s/ against /z/, /θ/ against /ð/.
Vowel length can break a rhyme.
Exam answers follow standard pronunciation.
content.takeaway: A single sound can turn a homophone into a near miss.

check.question: Which pair differ only in voicing?
check.why: Loose ends in /s/ and lose in /z/; the other three pairs are true homophones.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Rhyme is about sound after the stressed vowel. 'Love' and 'move' share four letters but no vowel sound, so they do not rhyme.

steps.result: Loose /luːs/ and lose /luːz/ differ in voicing; food /uː/ and foot /ʊ/ differ in length; advice /s/ and advise /z/ differ in voicing.

lessons.title: Word Stress
lessons.objective: Place stress on the correct syllable of polysyllabic words using word class, suffix and compound patterns.

content.heading: Word stress
paragraphs: A radio presenter says 'PREsent' for the gift and 'preSENT' for the verb, and listeners hear two different words. The difference is stress.

content.heading: Stress belongs to the word
paragraphs: Stress is the syllable a speaker makes louder, longer and higher. English does not mark it in spelling, so the same letters can carry different stress: a REcord is a file, but to reCORD is to store sound.

Monosyllables carry stress by default, so exam items use polysyllables. Two-syllable nouns and adjectives usually stress the first syllable (TAble, HAPpy, DOCtor), while two-syllable verbs usually stress the second (beGIN, reLAX, deCIDE).
Nigerian English sometimes places stress differently, as in 'MAintain' for mainTAIN. The exam follows standard British pronunciation, so learn the pattern rather than your own habit.
bullets: Stress means louder, longer and higher.
Nouns often front-stress; verbs often end-stress.
Spelling does not show stress.
content.takeaway: Stress is a property of the spoken word, not of its spelling.

check.question: As a noun, 'record' is stressed on the ______ syllable.
check.why: The noun REcord stresses the first syllable; the verb reCORD stresses the second.

content.heading: Suffixes move the stress
paragraphs: Adding a suffix can pull the stress to a different syllable. Photograph stresses the first syllable, photography the second, and photographic the third, although the letters are nearly the same.
Words ending in -tion, -sion, -ic, -ical, -ity and -ify usually stress the syllable just before the suffix: educate becomes eduCAtion, politics becomes poLItical, and real becomes reALity.
The rule explains why POlitics changes to poliTIcian and EConomy to ecoNOMic. Learn the word family together, because the exam often asks which word in a set is stressed differently.
bullets: -tion and -sion stress the syllable before.
-ic and -ical stress just before the suffix.
-ity and -ify pull the stress backwards too.
content.takeaway: A suffix usually pulls the stress to the syllable before it.

check.question: Where is the stress in 'photography'?
check.why: Photography is pho-TOG-ra-phy: the -graphy ending pulls the stress onto the second syllable.

visual.caption: The same spelling carries stress on the first syllable as a noun and the second as a verb.

content.heading: Compounds and contrasts
paragraphs: Compound nouns stress the first element: BLACKbird, FOOTball, TEApot and POST office. Compound adjectives and phrasal verbs often stress the second: well-KNOWN, old-FASHioned, underSTAND and turn OFF.

Stress can also distinguish meaning: a GREENhouse is a glass building, while a green HOUSE is a house painted green. The same contrast appears in 'English teacher' for a teacher of English and 'English TEACHER' for a teacher who is English.

In connected speech, stress falls on content words such as nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs, and weakens on articles, prepositions and auxiliaries. That sentence-level pattern is the subject of emphatic stress.
bullets: Compound nouns stress the first element.
Compound adjectives and phrasal verbs stress the second.
A stress shift can change the meaning.
content.takeaway: In a compound, the stressed element tells you which part is being named.

check.question: Which compound is stressed on its first element?
check.why: Blackbird is a compound noun, so it stresses BLACK; the others are an adjective and phrasal verbs that stress the second part.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn word families, not single words: photograph, photography and photographic together show the suffix rule at work.

steps.reason: The stress of the family is easier to see from the short form.
steps.result: Politics stresses the first syllable: POL-i-tics.

lessons.title: Emphatic Stress in Connected Speech
lessons.objective: Identify which word carries emphatic stress in a sentence and the question or correction that stress answers.

content.heading: Emphatic stress
paragraphs: A teacher says 'ADA wrote the letter', not 'Bola', and every student knows who wrote it. The emphasis does the work of a whole sentence.

content.heading: The stressed word is the correction
paragraphs: Emphatic stress is sentence-level stress placed on one word to contrast it with another. The stressed word answers the implied question or corrects a wrong assumption.
In 'ADA wrote the letter', the stress answers 'Who wrote the letter?'. In 'Ada WROTE the letter', it answers whether Ada wrote it rather than read or typed it.

The rest of the sentence is spoken more weakly, so the contrast is clear. In print, examiners often capitalise the stressed word or describe where the stress falls, and the capital letter is your cue.
bullets: Emphatic stress marks a contrast.
The stressed word answers the implied question.
Everything else in the sentence is weakened.
content.takeaway: Move the emphasis and you answer a different question.

check.question: 'Ada WROTE the letter' answers which question?
options: When did Ada write the letter?
check.why: The stress on WROTE corrects the doubt about the action, so it answers whether she wrote rather than read or typed it.

content.heading: Reading the question behind the stress
paragraphs: JAMB usually gives a sentence with one word capitalised and asks which question it answers, or gives a question and asks where the stress falls. Work from the contrast, not from loudness alone.
'Bola cooked RICE' answers 'What did Bola cook?', because rice is contrasted with other foods. 'BOLA cooked rice' answers 'Who cooked the rice?'.
A negative correction works the same way. 'He did not go to LAGOS' contradicts 'He went to Lagos', not 'He went to Abuja'; the stressed place is the one being denied.
bullets: Identify the word in contrast.
Match it to the question it answers.
A stressed negative denies that same item.
content.takeaway: Find the word in contrast, then read the question it answers.

check.question: 'Bola cooked RICE' answers which question?
check.why: The stress falls on the object, so it answers what was cooked rather than who cooked it.

content.heading: Word stress versus emphatic stress
paragraphs: Word stress lives inside a word and decides which syllable is strong; emphatic stress lives in a sentence and decides which word is strong. Confusing the two is the commonest oral-forms error.
The same sentence can shift emphasis without changing its words: 'I didn't say HE stole the book' denies that he was the thief, while 'I didn't say he STOLE the book' denies the theft.

Auxiliaries and prepositions can carry emphatic stress too. 'He IS coming' corrects doubt about the fact, and 'Put it ON the table' contrasts the place with another. The same words can therefore answer different questions as the emphasis moves.
bullets: Word stress chooses a syllable.
Emphatic stress chooses a word.
Any word can be emphasised, even a preposition.
content.takeaway: Word stress chooses a syllable; emphatic stress chooses a word.

check.question: Emphatic stress is best described as ______.
options: stress on one syllable of a word
stress on one word to show contrast
stress on the last word of every sentence
check.why: Emphatic stress highlights one word in an utterance so that it contrasts with another word or answers a specific question.

visual.caption: Word stress chooses a syllable; emphatic stress chooses a word.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Do not look for the longest word. The stressed word is the one that would change if the speaker were correcting a different mistake.
